rationale: The Prolangs-C++ 'life' benchmark is a small, compute-bound cellular-automata simulation with tight, hot inner loops over a fixed grid, so per-instruction and per-block expansions (BCF) are heavily cost-penalized (high RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights) to keep them off the hottest functions while still being available where features justify them; control-flow flattening (FLA) offers the strongest reverse-engineering resistance for the short, branchy update/neighbor-count routines, so it gets the highest SecurityGain with a moderate runtime penalty to reserve it for the most security-favored functions; SUB is cheap and effective on the arithmetic-heavy neighbor counting and gets strong weights with minimal cost penalties; SPLIT and ICALL are low-overhead diversity multipliers that also amplify FLA/SUB effectiveness, so DiversityGain is prioritized; IBR provides good resistance via indirect branching but carries moderate overhead and correctness risk on the hot simulation loop, so it is balanced; IGV adds cheap global-access indirection suitable for the grid/state arrays. Overall the table biases toward high SecurityGain/DiversityGain on low-cost passes while using elevated RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights to gate the expensive structural passes away from the hot loops, keeping total overhead acceptable with low correctness risk across the board.
